newsitem.title: ITALY: Olivetti worries grow ahead of meetings.
newsitem.headline: Olivetti worries grow ahead of meetings.

text.p: Shares in Olivetti slipped lower again on Wednesday as investors fretted over a critical internal auditors' report and spiralling debt levels at the struggling Italian information technology group.

The report expressed concern with certain items in Olivetti's first-half results, casting doubt over its capital gain from selling a stake in British-based computer group Acorn and questioning its commercial credit arrangements.

This criticism came as Olivetti produced 150 pages of details on its first-half 1996 results, indicating its debt had almost doubled over the months of July and August due to the seasonality of payments to suppliers and restructuring costs.
In Italy, internal auditors act like independent consultants attending key company meetings, giving their own reports on group results and working in conjunction with external auditors.
The internal auditors say that in their report following Olivetti's first-half 1996 results they were assisted by the company's external auditors, Coopers & Lybrand.

Analysts are hoping that Olivetti's management, led by new chief executive Roberto Colaninno, will be able to answer the questions hanging over the accounts when it meets analysts in Milan on Thursday and in London the following day.
"This is pretty serious for Olivetti as the internal auditors are now posing questions over the financial affairs of the company," said one industry analyst in Milan.

The report was a nasty reminder for Olivetti's hard-pressed investors of the events of a month ago, when its ex-director general in charge of finance and auditing, Renzo Francesconi, resigned after questioning the accuracy of the group's accounts.

The internal auditors' 14-page report was published this week after the group confirmed late on Monday that it made a first-half 1996 pretax loss of 440.2 billion lire ($290 million) and said its net debt rose to 2.39 trillion lire at the end of August from 1.26 trillion at June 30.

Olivetti shares were weak throughout the day and closed 1.53 percent down at 520.3 lire on a generally firmer Milan stock market after dropping 5.9 percent on Tuesday -- a long way from the 1,280 lire level at the start of the year.
The report questioned whether a capital gain of 64 billion lire in Olivetti's first-half results, after it sold a 14.7 percent stake in Acorn to Lehman Brothers International, was entirely secure.
The sum is currently deposited with Lehman and will be made over to Olivetti's Telemedia company in instalments as the shares are placed by Lehmans on the open market.

The report also critised Olivetti's commercial credit arrangements over a loan of 46.2 billion lire by its Olivetti Systems and Networks unit which the auditors say should have appeared on the group's balance sheet.
"There are a lot of questions surrounding Olivetti. We hope they will attempt to answer some of them later this week," said one London-based analyst.

The report also pointed out that auditors would like to have seen more details of how the group intended to use a 200 billion lire restructuring charge given with its first-half results. ($1=1,516 lire)
